Every man ostracised in ancient Athens w.why: The defining term of the procedure, given in the first sentence of the Wikipedia article and in every account of it. No exception: men recalled early (Aristides, Xanthippus, Cimon) had still been sentenced to ten years, which is why the rule speaks of the sentence.

Hipparchus, son of Charmus, was sentence.why: People say that Athens ostracised men for ten years and that Hipparchus son of Charmus was the first man ostracised. Nobody gives his term with his name, though it is true; only the class rule does. Writers state the rule once, for the whole class of ostracised men, and do not repeat the term for each man.

notes: Dev TBox contraction paired with history-replace-d005: removes that revision's original rule, 'Every man ostracised in ancient Athens was sentenced to ten years of exile' (same relation, sentenced_to_exile_for). The rule is the defining term of ostracism and has no exception once stated as the sentence. Its own questions (direct, paraphrase, cross-lingual, propositional) become 'does not know'; under strong Kleene the three propositional answers are unknown. The three derived queries are the revision's, asked of the original rule: Hipparchus son of Charmus, Megacles son of Hippocrates and Menon son of Meneclides, each stated as ostracised in the prompt (inheritance, 2 hops): the term (ten years), whether the sentence had run out after seven years (no) and his age at the end if he left at 40 (50); after the removal nothing gives any of them. The well-known victims (Aristides, Themistocles, Cimon) are not asked. Near unrelated asks another Athenian sentence (Socrates': death); contraction is exempt from Rule 7. Evidence is the paired revision's.
